root_cause: The Node.js N-API bindings test file src/bindings/js/node/tests/unit/infer_request.test.js aborted with glibc's 'malloc_consolidate(): unaligned fastbin chunk detected' heap-corruption detector, triggered right after the 'original TypedArray is alive during infer()' subtest in the 'GC safety infer() / inferAsync()' describe block (lines 449-505). That suite repeatedly allocates Float32Array buffers, wraps them in ov.Tensor, and runs multiple concurrent infer()/inferAsync() calls specifically to stress native buffer-lifetime/GC-pinning behavior in the InferRequest/Tensor N-API bindings (src/bindings/js/node/src/infer_request.cpp, src/bindings/js/node/include/infer_request.hpp). glibc's fastbin-chunk check firing here indicates a native heap-corrupting bug (e.g., double free, out-of-bounds write, or use-after-free on a TypedArray-backed buffer) in that wrapping/reference-keeping code, exercised by async/GC timing. The failing PR (#39148) only touches src/plugins/intel_gpu (sdpa_micro.cl GPU kernel and a GPU unit test) and runs CPU inference in this JS test, so the PR diff is unrelated to the crash; this is the same test suite flagged in a prior investigation (signature_hash 64286f1d490ba863, SIGSEGV) for a likely related native memory-lifetime bug, but the specific glibc abort signature differs (heap corruption vs. segfault) so it is tracked as a separate pattern.
reproduction_steps: Build the Node.js bindings (src/bindings/js/node) for OpenVINO on Linux, then from that directory run `node --test tests/unit/infer_request.test.js` repeatedly (ideally in a loop, e.g. 20-50x) focusing on the 'GC safety infer() / inferAsync()' describe block (lines 449-505 of the test file). The corruption is timing/GC-dependent and may not reproduce on every run; running under glibc with MALLOC_CHECK_=3 or under valgrind/ASan will surface the faulting write more reliably than the bare 'malloc_consolidate' abort message.
recommended_actions: Re-run the failed 'OpenVINO JS API (26) / OpenVINO JS API' job; if it passes on retry this supports a timing-dependent (GC/async-scheduling) native memory bug rather than a deterministic one.
Run the Node JS bindings test suite under AddressSanitizer or valgrind in a diagnostic CI lane to get an exact faulting write location in src/bindings/js/node/src/infer_request.cpp / tensor.cpp.

Audit how ov.Tensor/InferRequest N-API bindings keep the backing ArrayBuffer/TypedArray alive across concurrent infer()/inferAsync() calls (Napi::Reference lifetime, finalizer callbacks) for double-free or buffer-overrun bugs, particularly around the newly added GC-safety test scenarios.
Add core-dump / sanitizer-based CI diagnostics for this job so future glibc heap-corruption aborts include an actual backtrace instead of only the bare 'malloc_consolidate' message.
prevention_strategies: Run new native-memory-lifetime stress tests (like the 'GC safety' suite) multiple times under ASan/valgrind before merging, since GC/async-timing-dependent heap corruption is often intermittent and easy to miss in a single CI pass. Add persistent core-dump/sanitizer tooling to the JS API CI job so any future native abort (SIGSEGV, SIGABRT, malloc_consolidate) yields a stack trace automatically.
historical_context: Pattern 64286f1d490ba863 (count 1 prior to this run) recorded a SIGSEGV crash in the exact same 'GC safety infer() / inferAsync()' suite of infer_request.test.js on run 41502170440 (PR #39321), also unrelated to that PR's actual diff. This occurrence shows a different glibc abort signature (malloc_consolidate heap corruption) in the same suite, consistent with an underlying native buffer-lifetime bug in the N-API Tensor/InferRequest bindings; tracked as a new, distinct pattern (a59d13e7e8bb25d4) because the manifestation differs, but both point at the same component.
